abstract: |
  The European Union prices the carbon its power plants and factories emit, but not most of the carbon in what Europeans buy, 40 percent of which is emitted abroad. This paper proposes a carbon consumption tax in two parts: a carbon component of VAT, charged on every good and service consumed in the Union at rebuttable default intensities while the value component falls, and a legal obligation, fixed a decade ahead, on the few suppliers of fuel for homes and vehicles. I show that, with full input crediting, each firm pays the carbon price on the carbon it adds and the consumer bears it on the whole supply chain; that exempt stages break the chain; and that deducting carbon prices paid upstream gives every tonne one price. Input–output calibration puts the taxable household basket at 0.41 kg CO₂e per euro in 2022, imports at twice EU-made goods. A rule that cuts the value component by last year's carbon receipts keeps the swap revenue-neutral. The swap is mildly regressive: at €200 per tonne the poorest fifth pays 0.4 percent of spending more and the richest 0.2 percent less.

*Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.6. Version 0.1 (2026) proposed country-level intensity scores and adoption under Article 192 TFEU; this version replaces both.*

*Keywords:* carbon pricing; consumption-based emissions; value-added tax; destination basis; border carbon adjustment; EU law. *JEL:* H23, H25, F18, Q54, Q58.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

The EU prices carbon where it is emitted, and much of the carbon Europeans cause is emitted somewhere the EU cannot price. The Emissions Trading System (ETS) covers power and heavy industry inside the Union, and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) extends that price to imports of cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen [@CBAMReg]. Nothing prices the carbon in an imported shirt, phone or sofa. In 2022 the final demand of EU residents caused 3.7 Gt of greenhouse gases along global supply chains, plus 0.7 Gt that households emitted directly from boilers and cars [@EurostatGHGFP]. On my calculation (@sec-defaults), 40 percent of the carbon embodied in what households buy subject to VAT was emitted outside the EU, and those imports embody about twice as much carbon per euro as EU-made goods. A price on production leaves that carbon unpriced and makes producing in Europe dearer than producing elsewhere for sale in Europe [@PetersHertwich2008; @Peters2011; @DavisCaldeira2010].

Production pricing is also near its political limits. Explicit carbon prices cover about 28 percent of global emissions, at an emissions-weighted average of about \$5 per tonne once unpriced emissions count as zero [@WorldBank2025], against a social cost of carbon estimated at \$185 per tonne [@Rennert2022]. Inside the EU, a higher price on production meets the objection that it handicaps exporters, and a new price on households meets the cost-of-living objection that has already delayed ETS2 [@ETS2Dir]. A consumption price that replaces part of an existing tax, rather than adding a new one, answers both: it does not fall on exports, and it need not raise the average tax on consumption.

The question is how the EU could price the carbon in consumption, wherever it is emitted, using institutions it already has. The answer proposed here has two parts. The first is a *carbon component* of VAT. Each registered business charges, on its sales, a carbon price per tonne of the embodied carbon in what it sells, and credits the carbon component on its purchases, exactly as it credits VAT. Embodied carbon is read from a published *default intensity* for the product category, the same for every origin, unless the seller proves a lower figure. Exports are zero-rated and imports are charged at the border. As the carbon component rises, the existing *value component* of VAT falls, by a rule that keeps the swap revenue-neutral. The second part is a *forward obligation*: a legal duty, written into law ten years ahead with a published price floor, on the few firms that supply road and heating fuel to pay for the carbon they sell. Fuel burned in homes and cars never passes through a goods chain, so VAT cannot reach it.

The paper makes four contributions.

1. **The VAT-chain result** (@sec-chain). With full crediting, each firm remits the carbon price on the carbon it adds, and the final consumer bears it on the whole supply chain (Proposition 1). An exempt stage breaks the chain and makes upstream carbon cascade (Proposition 2). Deducting carbon prices paid upstream, under the ETS, CBAM, the forward obligation or a recognized foreign scheme, gives each tonne exactly one price (Proposition 3).
2. **Calibrated defaults** (@sec-defaults). A multi-regional input–output calculation from Eurostat's FIGARO tables gives default intensities for 23 product categories. The taxable household basket embodied 0.41 kg CO₂e per euro in 2022; goods from outside the EU embodied 0.76, against 0.38 for EU-made goods and services.
3. **A neutrality rule** (@sec-fiscal). Cutting the value component each year by the previous year's net carbon receipts keeps the swap revenue-neutral without forecasting decarbonization. On the illustrative path to €200 per tonne in 2037, the value component ends between 10.8 and 12.7 percent, not at the 10 percent of a fixed path.
4. **A legal map** (@sec-legal). The carbon component is a change to the VAT system and needs unanimity under Article 113 TFEU; Article 192(2)(a) does not avoid this. The forward obligation can be adopted by qualified majority, as ETS2 was.

The closest prior work is the proposal for a consumption charge on carbon-intensive materials [@Ismer2016; @PollittNeuhoffLin2020; @Neuhoff2026]. That charge covers a handful of basic materials, such as steel and cement, and is levied as an excise outside VAT. The carbon component covers every taxable good and service and runs through the VAT invoice chain with credit for input carbon, so each firm pays only on the carbon it adds and exports are relieved without separate machinery. It shares the materials charge's choice of standardized values, the same for every origin, and adds the rebuttal that rewards clean exporters.

The paper is the consumption track of the series' two-track architecture [@CFPB11]. Production is priced separately by a revenue-neutral feebate on emissions intensity [@CFPB12]; recognition of foreign carbon prices at the border is developed in @CFPB13 and the measurement framework in @CFPB61. @sec-distribution reports the distributional effects, @sec-obligation the forward obligation, and @sec-admin administration and fraud.

# Related literature {#sec-literature}

The paper connects five literatures; Appendix A reviews them in detail.

*Consumption-based accounting.* High-income economies are net importers of embodied carbon. Emissions in traded goods rose from 20 to 26 percent of the global total between 1990 and 2008, and net transfers from developing to developed countries rose from 0.4 to 1.6 GtCO₂ [@Peters2011]; in several European countries more than 30 percent of consumption-based emissions are imported [@DavisCaldeira2010]. Pricing all embodied emissions is not first-best, because a tonne imported is not a tonne added globally [@JakobSteckelEdenhofer2014]. The case for a consumption charge rests instead on leakage, administration and acceptability.

*Consumption charges on carbon-intensive materials.* The closest prior work is the proposal for a consumption charge, or "climate contribution", on carbon-intensive materials, levied at benchmark intensity on domestic and imported products alike. @Ismer2016 designed it legally, as an excise-type liability; @PollittNeuhoffLin2020 modeled it, finding that at about €80/tCO₂ it adds about 10 percent to EU CO₂ cuts by 2050 with no leakage; @Grubb2022 placed it among three trade-compatible options and argued that defaults by product category are feasible if they apply to imports and domestic goods alike; and @Neuhoff2026 restate it with standardized values, the same for every origin, to stop exporters shuffling their cleanest output to the EU. @McAuslandNajjar2015 and @EichnerPethig2015 analyze carbon footprint taxes formally. This paper's contribution is the vehicle: running the charge through the VAT invoice chain, with credit for input carbon, across every taxable good and service rather than a few materials.

*Destination-based taxation and VAT.* For a uniform tax, origin and destination bases are equivalent in their real effects [@LockwoodDeMezaMyles1994]; @LockwoodWhalley2010 apply the point to carbon border adjustments. It follows that VAT's value component, being uniform, carries no carbon incentive. The World Bank's total carbon price therefore excludes general VAT, counting only preferential VAT rates on fuels, as subsidies [@Agnolucci2023]. The carbon component is what turns part of VAT into a carbon price. VAT, now levied in most of the world, shows that the destination basis works at scale [@KeenLockwood2010]; destination-based business taxes rest on the same logic [@Devereux2021].

*Border adjustment and trade law.* The design literature sets out the choices of coverage, measurement and treatment of exports [@IsmerNeuhoff2007; @Mehling2019; @KeenParryRoaf2022]. @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend domestic benchmarks first and country-specific values later. @Mattoo2009 find that a border tax on the carbon content of imports, measured at the exporter's own intensity, would cut China's manufacturing exports by about a fifth, while one based on domestic carbon content would do far less damage. @Evans2021 note that a border adjustment on imports alone leaves exporters exposed; a VAT-based charge zero-rates exports by construction.

*Credibility.* Governments cannot bind successors to future tax rates, so firms discount announced carbon prices [@KydlandPrescott1977; @LaffontTirole1996]. @HelmHepburnMash2003 proposed delegating carbon policy to an independent body; @Brunner2012 compare commitment devices; @ChiappinelliNeuhoff2020 show that carbon contracts for difference can make a government willing to "tie its hands". The forward obligation applies the same idea to fuel suppliers.

*Leakage and distribution.* Model studies find leakage of 5–25 percent of the emission cuts without border adjustment and −5 to 15 percent with it [@BrangerQuirion2014], while ex-post studies find no detectable leakage from the ETS so far [@NaegeleZaklan2019; @Dechezlepretre2022]: the case for a destination charge concerns the higher prices ahead, not the past. @Holland2012 shows that, when regulation is incomplete, an intensity standard paired with a consumption tax can reach the first best, which is the formal case for pairing this paper's consumption track with a production feebate. Household carbon is a necessity, with an income elasticity below one [@Sager2019], and a consumption-based EU carbon price is roughly neutral within member states but regressive across them [@Feindt2021].

*What is new.* The literature has the destination principle, the consumption charge on materials, the default-value approach and the credibility argument. It does not have a carbon charge run through the VAT chain with input crediting, a statement of when that chain prices each firm's carbon added and when it fails, a calibration of defaults for the whole taxable basket, a rule that keeps the swap neutral, or an analysis of the design choice that decides whether a national version is a prohibited turnover tax. Those are this paper's contributions.

# The carbon component in the VAT chain {#sec-chain}

This section shows that a carbon price credited through the VAT chain taxes each firm's carbon added, as VAT taxes value added, and states the conditions.

**Setup.** A good passes through $n$ stages. Stage $k$ buys the output of stage $k-1$, adds value $w_k$ and emits $a_k$ tonnes of CO₂e itself, its *carbon added*. Its sales value net of tax is $p_k = p_{k-1} + w_k$, and the *embodied carbon* of its output is $E_k = \sum_{j \le k} a_j$. The value component of VAT has rate $v$; the carbon component has price $P$ per tonne. Each firm's invoice states a *carbon base* $C_k$ in tonnes: either a default, $C_k = d_k\, p_k$, where $d_k$ is the published intensity per euro for its product category, or a verified figure. Firm $k$ remits
$$
T_k = v\,(p_k - p_{k-1}) + P\,(C_k - C_{k-1}),
$$ {#eq-remit}
charging tax on its sales and crediting the tax on its purchases. Some firms also pay an explicit carbon price $q_k$ per tonne on their own emissions: the ETS price, a CBAM certificate, the forward obligation of @sec-obligation, or a recognized foreign carbon price.

**Proposition 1 (carbon added).** *With full crediting at every stage: (i) total carbon-component receipts are $P\,C_n$, whatever the carbon bases at earlier stages; (ii) if every stage's base equals its embodied carbon, $C_k = E_k$, each firm remits $P\,a_k$, the carbon price on its carbon added; (iii) the final consumer then bears $P\,E_n$, the carbon price on the good's whole supply chain.*

The proof, in Appendix B, is a telescoping sum. Three implications matter for design. First, only the base at the final sale fixes what the consumer pays; earlier bases decide only who remits and when, as with VAT. Second, the base must fall per euro along the chain, because later stages add value with little carbon. In the worked example below the embodied intensity is 2.0 kg per euro at the steel mill and 0.65 kg per euro at the till. A single per-euro default applied at every stage would overcharge at retail by the ratio of retail to producer value; this is why @tbl-defaults reports defaults both at basic prices, for the border and producer stages, and at purchasers' prices, for retail. Third, a firm whose output base is smaller than its input base, $C_k < C_{k-1}$, is due a refund, the same opening that VAT refund fraud exploits (@sec-admin). Defaults should therefore be consistent along a chain, so that published bases never imply negative carbon added.

*Incentives.* Under defaults alone, a firm's charge does not depend on its own emissions, so the carbon component shifts demand between product categories but gives no reason to cut intensity within one. That incentive comes from rebuttal. A seller that verifies $C_k = E_k$ below the default lowers its customers' tax and gains market share; the clean producer then faces a marginal price of $P$ per tonne on goods sold in the EU. Rebuttal is optional, so only producers below the default use it. The default must therefore be set no lower than the average it replaces, or dirty producers keep the undercharge (@sec-defaults).

**Proposition 2 (exempt stages).** *Let stage $j$ be exempt: it charges no tax on its sales and cannot credit tax on its purchases, so its input taxes $v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}$ become a cost in its price. (i) If $j = n$, the consumer bears the carbon price on upstream carbon, $P\,E_{n-1}$, once, but the exempt firm's own carbon $a_n$ goes uncharged by the carbon component. (ii) If $j < n$ and later bases are correct, the consumer pays $(1+v)\,(v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1})$ more than under full crediting: carbon upstream of the exempt stage is charged twice, and the value component is charged on the tax embedded in the exempt firm's price.*

Exemption breaks the carbon chain exactly as it breaks the VAT chain. Financial services, insurance, letting of housing, health, education and social care are exempt under Articles 132 and 135 of the VAT Directive [@VATDirective], and public bodies are largely outside its scope. Together they made up 31 percent of EU household spending in 2022 (@tbl-defaults), and their own carbon intensity is low, 0.06–0.10 kg CO₂e per euro. Final-stage exemption therefore leaves little carbon unpriced: a hospital's boiler is reached by the forward obligation instead. The cascade in case (ii) matters where exempt firms sell to taxable ones, as banks and insurers do. Two remedies already exist in VAT: the option to tax certain exempt supplies, and zero-rating with a right of deduction, which restores Proposition 1.

**Proposition 3 (one price per tonne).** *Let each invoice carry, besides the carbon base, the carbon price already paid, $Q_k = \sum_{j \le k} \min(q_j, P)\, a_j$, and let the carbon component on a sale be $P\,E_k - Q_k$. Then firm $k$ remits $(P - \min(q_k, P))\,a_k$, and every tonne bears a total price of $\max(P, q_k)$: exactly $P$ wherever upstream prices do not exceed it.*

The table below works through a three-stage chain in 2032 (@fig-chain in Appendix B plots it), when the carbon price on the illustrative path is €100 per tonne and the value component 12.5 percent. A steel mill emits 400 kg in making €200 of steel and pays the ETS at a stylized €80 per tonne, €32. An appliance maker turns the steel into a €500 appliance, adding 100 kg; a retailer sells it for €800, adding 20 kg. The value component raises 12.5 percent of €800, €100, split by value added. The carbon component raises €20: the mill remits €8 ($40 - 32$), the maker €10 and the retailer €2. With the ETS payment, the 520 kg in the appliance bear €52, exactly €100 per tonne.

| Stage | Sales value (€) | Carbon added (kg) | Embodied (kg/€) | Value component (€) | ETS paid (€) | Carbon component (€) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Steel mill | 200 | 400 | 2.00 | 25.0 | 32 | 8 |
| Appliance maker | 500 | 100 | 1.00 | 37.5 | 0 | 10 |
| Retailer | 800 | 20 | 0.65 | 37.5 | 0 | 2 |
| Total | | 520 | | 100.0 | 32 | 20 |

: Worked example: a carbon component in a three-stage chain, 2032 (stylized). Value component 12.5 percent; carbon price €100/tCO₂e; ETS price €80/t at the mill, deducted under Proposition 3. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/check_propositions.py`.

Proposition 3 states the link to the production track [@CFPB11]. Deductions count explicit prices paid per tonne, averaged over the sector that paid them. A revenue-neutral feebate charges dirty producers and rebates clean ones, so its average net price is zero and it earns no deduction: a good made under a feebate pays the full carbon component at consumption, while the feebate supplies the marginal incentive at production. Exports are zero-rated, so the exporter reclaims the carbon component on its inputs and its output carries only the production-track price, which is 1.1's equivalence result (Proposition 1 of @CFPB11) restated through the VAT chain. The deduction must be capped at $P$ per tonne: without the cap, a tonne priced at more than $P$ upstream would draw a refund from the carbon component. Where an exempt firm sits in the chain (Proposition 2), it issues no carbon invoice, so carbon prices paid upstream of it are lost to the deduction as well and the cascade is larger still.

*Imports and exports.* An imported good enters the chain at the border. The importer pays the carbon component on the customs value at the default for its category, less any CBAM price paid on the same tonnes, and credits it in its next return, as it credits import VAT; from there Proposition 1 applies unchanged. An exporter zero-rates its sales and reclaims the carbon component on its inputs, so the export leaves carrying no EU consumption charge. Proposition 1(i) gives the system the self-enforcing property of VAT. An importer that understates value or intensity at the border lowers its own payment, but not what the consumer pays: the retailer still charges the retail default on the retail value, and the shortfall is collected from the firms in between, which have no input credit to offset it. The final-sale default is the main line of defense, as the retail rate is for VAT. Under verification the property weakens, because a verified base downstream builds on carbon declared upstream, which is why verified claims need audit (@sec-admin).

*An exempt stage in numbers.* Take a bank that buys €10,000 of computers embodying 3 tonnes of CO₂e in 2032, when the carbon price is €100. It cannot credit the €300 carbon component, which becomes a cost of its services. If it sells those services to a taxable manufacturer, the €300 sits in the manufacturer's costs but on no invoice it can credit, while the manufacturer's own sales carry a default that already counts the carbon in its suppliers' computers. The 3 tonnes are charged twice, and the value component is charged once more on the €300. The sums are small, because banks are not carbon-intensive, but the pattern is the familiar cost of VAT exemptions.

# Default intensities and rebuttal {#sec-defaults}

The default intensities are the whole design: they fix the base for every seller that does not verify, which at the start is nearly all of them. This section calibrates them, sets the rule for imports and rebuttal, and checks them against trade law.

**Method.** I built an environmentally extended multi-regional input–output model from Eurostat's FIGARO inter-country table for 2022, which covers 49 economies plus the rest of the world and 64 products [@EurostatFIGARO], and Eurostat's greenhouse gas emissions by country and industry from its footprint dataset [@EurostatGHGFP]. Multipliers give the CO₂-equivalent embodied per euro of each country's output of each product; EU household purchases weight them into intensities by category and origin. The model reproduces Eurostat's own estimate of the EU footprint to within 0.2 percent (3,749 against 3,743 Mt CO₂e, excluding households' direct emissions). Appendix C gives the details and the code.

@tbl-defaults reports the result for 23 categories. Intensities at basic prices apply at the border and between firms. Intensities at purchasers' prices spread households' purchases of wholesale and retail trade services, 64 percent of the basic value of the goods they buy, across those goods, and apply at the final sale.

Four results stand out. First, the taxable household basket embodied 0.41 kg CO₂e per euro, or 0.29 kg if only CO₂ is counted. That is well above the 0.25 kg per euro at which the illustrative path of the brief and of v0.1 is neutral, so the fixed path would have raised revenue at the start, not lost it (@sec-fiscal). Second, imports from outside the EU embodied 0.76 kg per euro against 0.38 for EU-made goods and services, and the gap is widest for furniture (3.0 times), electronics (2.3), machinery (2.5) and textiles (2.1) (@fig-defaults). Third, the categories most charged per euro are electricity, flights, farm products and fuel, which are also those where the forward obligation and the ETS already apply, so the deduction of Proposition 3 matters most there. Fourth, methane and nitrous oxide triple the intensity of farm products (0.81 against 0.27 kg CO₂ only, at purchasers' prices). Pricing CO₂ alone would exempt most of the carbon in food.

![Embodied greenhouse gas intensity by product category, EU-made and imported from outside the EU, 2022. The high value for imported water and waste services rests on a tiny import share. Source: as @tbl-defaults; `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig1-default-intensities.png){#fig-defaults width=100%}

The calibration is a starting point, not a schedule ready to legislate. FIGARO's 64 products are coarser than customs categories: "electronics" covers both a phone and a cable. Defaults per euro also fall with inflation, by 12 percent between 2022 and 2023 on the same method, partly through decarbonization and partly through prices. The legislated schedule would be built at a finer level, the 4- or 6-digit level of the Combined Nomenclature for goods, where customs data also allow defaults per physical unit, as CBAM does per tonne of steel [@CBAMReg], and it would be updated each year.

**Imports: the same default for every origin.** The default for each category should be the EU average intensity at basic prices, applied to every origin. Three reasons support one default per category rather than country-specific values. It treats like products alike whatever their source, which is the strongest position under the national-treatment rule for internal taxes in GATT Article III:2 [@IsmerNeuhoff2007; @Mehling2019]. It avoids the trade shock that @Mattoo2009 find from charging imports at the exporter's own intensity. And it removes the gain from resource shuffling, sending the cleanest output to the EU, which origin-specific values invite [@Neuhoff2026]. The cost is that imports are undercharged at first. On @tbl-defaults, an EU-average default charges imports at about half their embodied carbon. That is a price worth paying to avoid a trade dispute in the first years, and the gap closes as rebuttal and tightening proceed.

**Rebuttal turns the defaults into an incentive.** An importer or producer whose verified intensity is below the default pays on its own figure. Take a €100 phone imported in 2032, when the carbon price is €100 per tonne. The default for electronics at basic prices, the EU-made average, is 0.28 kg CO₂e per euro, so the importer pays €2.80. Electronics imported from outside the EU average 0.63 kg per euro, and Chinese-made electronics 0.84 (`2.Source/defaults_by_category.csv`), so the default undercharges the average import by €3.50 and the Chinese one by €5.60. An exporter that verifies 0.15 kg per euro pays €1.50 and gains €1.30 a phone over its rivals on the default; one at 0.84 has no reason to verify. The verification standard should be plant- or firm-wide intensity for the product, not consignment-level figures, so that a clean line cannot be reserved for EU buyers [@Neuhoff2026]. The verification infrastructure already exists for CBAM goods, whose monitoring rules and accredited verifiers could extend to other categories over time. Once importers charge embodied carbon at verified intensity, an exporter's most competitive policy at home is a production feebate at the same rate (Proposition 7 of @CFPB11), which turns competition toward lower carbon.

**Tightening.** Defaults can move from the EU average toward origin-specific values, with a deduction for carbon prices paid abroad as CBAM allows [@CBAMReg; @CFPB13], once verified data cover enough of each category. @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend the same sequence: domestic benchmarks first, country-specific values later.

**Governance.** The Commission would publish the schedule each year by implementing act under the amending Directive, on a published method and data, with intensities per euro indexed to prices and, where customs data allow, per physical unit. Member states would not set their own defaults: a lower default for a member state's own producers would be a covert subsidy, the problem v0.1's national scores created in reverse. A category's default should change only once a year and by a published formula, so that firms can invoice on it with certainty.

**Trade law.** The carbon component is an internal tax on products, applied equally to domestic and imported goods and adjustable at the border under GATT Articles II:2(a) and III:2. The open question is whether embodied carbon, a characteristic of how a product was made, can differentiate otherwise like products; a pen made with coal power and one made with solar power are physically identical [@Mehling2019]. A default that is the same for every origin sidesteps the question for products that do not rebut, because like products then bear the same tax. Rebuttal raises it only in the direction GATT permits: an imported product can pay less than the default, never more than a like domestic product would.

# Fiscal design: the carbon charge partly replaces VAT {#sec-fiscal}

The carbon component should replace part of the value component, by a rule rather than by a fixed path, because the base it taxes is shrinking at an unknown rate.

**Scale.** EU member states raised €1,198 billion of VAT in 2022, 7.4 percent of GDP [@EurostatTax]. Taxable household spending, the core of the base, was €5.1 trillion at basic prices (@tbl-defaults). Each percentage point of the value component on that base is worth €51 billion; the half point a year on the illustrative path is worth €26 billion. A carbon price of €20 per tonne on the taxable basket at 0.41 kg per euro raises €42 billion before deductions. The base is narrower than total household spending of €8.2 trillion at purchasers' prices [@EurostatCOICOP] because rents, finance, health and education are exempt, and the Commission puts revenue forgone through exemptions and reduced rates, the VAT policy gap, at €742 billion in 2023 [@VATGap2025].

**Break-even intensity.** On the illustrative path the value component falls 0.5 points a year from 15 percent in 2027 and the carbon price rises €20 a year to €200 in 2037. A carbon price $P$ on a good of intensity $e$ kg per euro adds $Pe/10$ percentage points, so the two changes cancel at 0.25 kg per euro. Whether the swap raises or loses money depends on the basket's intensity net of deductions in each year (@tbl-fiscal).

| Basket intensity in 2037 (kg CO₂e/€) | 0.15 | 0.20 | 0.25 | 0.30 | 0.41 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Carbon component receipts, gross (points of base) | 3.00 | 4.00 | 5.00 | 6.00 | 8.24 |
| Receipts net of ETS deduction (points of base) | 2.66 | 3.55 | 4.44 | 5.33 | 7.31 |
| Revenue-neutral value component (%) | 12.3 | 11.5 | 10.6 | 9.7 | 7.7 |
| Revenue change on the fixed path, value component 10% (points) | −2.3 | −1.5 | −0.6 | +0.3 | +2.3 |
| … in € billion (2022 base of €5.1 trillion) | −120 | −74 | −29 | +17 | +119 |

: Fiscal effect of a €200/tCO₂e carbon component in 2037 by the intensity of the taxable basket. The ETS deduction applies to the 28 percent of the basket's footprint emitted by EU power and energy-intensive industry, at a stylized ETS price of €80/t. The last column is the 2022 intensity. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`. {#tbl-fiscal}

The basket's intensity in 2037 is unknown within a factor of two. It fell 12 percent per euro between 2022 and 2023, partly through inflation; the EU's targets imply continued falls in real terms; and the carbon component itself shifts spending toward cleaner goods. A fixed path from 15 to 10 percent loses €120 billion a year if the basket reaches 0.15 kg per euro and gains €119 billion if it stays at 0.41. Neither outcome is the "approximately neutral" path v0.1 claimed.

**The neutrality rule.** Each year's value component should equal its starting rate less the previous year's net carbon-component receipts as a share of the base:
$$
v_t = v_0 - \frac{R_{t-1}}{B_{t-1}}, \qquad R_t = \sum_i \big(P_t\,C_{i,t} - Q_{i,t}\big),
$$ {#eq-rule}
where $R_t$ is carbon-component revenue after the deductions of Proposition 3 and $B_t$ the taxable base. The rule needs no forecast. Revenue in year $t$ differs from the starting yield only by the growth of carbon receipts within the year, which shrinks as the carbon price stops rising. Each member state applies it to its own receipts, so no revenue moves between member states (@sec-distribution). The carbon charge then replaces VAT by whatever share the basket's carbon supports: about a fifth of the value component in the central case.

Because each member state applies the rule to its own receipts, the value cut differs with the carbon intensity of its households' spending. At €200 per tonne and 2022 intensities, before ETS deductions, the revenue-neutral cut would range from 7.0 points of taxable spending in Luxembourg and 7.5 in France to 8.7 in Poland and Slovakia and 8.9 in Bulgaria (`2.Source/distribution_countries.csv`). Member states with more carbon-intensive spending cut VAT more: their households pay more carbon component and get more back. The rule's one-year lag errs toward a small surplus while the carbon price rises, of 0.1–0.6 points of the base, €6–28 billion a year across the EU in the three scenarios of @fig-rule. A member state that prefers exact neutrality can cut the value component by the previous year's receipts scaled up by the rise in the carbon price.

@fig-rule shows the rule at work. If the basket's intensity falls 5 percent a year from its 2022 level, the value component falls to 13.5 percent in 2032 and 11.8 percent in 2037, and a good breaks even at 0.16 kg per euro in 2037. If intensity falls 3 percent a year, the value component ends at 10.8 percent; at 7 percent a year, 12.7 percent. Goods at 0.10 kg per euro then pay 13.8 percent in 2037 and goods at 0.80 kg per euro 27.8 percent, against 15 percent for both today.

![The neutrality rule. A: value component when it falls each year by the previous year's net carbon receipts, for three rates of decline in basket intensity, against the fixed path. B: total VAT rate on goods of given intensity in the central case. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig2-neutrality-rule.png){#fig-rule width=100%}

**The 15 percent floor binds.** Article 97 of the VAT Directive requires a standard rate of at least 15 percent [@VATDirective; @VATRateMin2018]. A clean good paying 13.8 percent breaches it, and so may the value component itself. The floor should be restated as applying to the sum of the two components on a good at the default intensity of the taxable basket, or the path should start from each member state's standard rate, all of which exceed 15 percent; Luxembourg's 17 percent is the lowest [VERIFY: national standard rates in 2026, Taxes in Europe Database].

**Reduced rates.** The carbon component should apply on top of reduced rates. Directive (EU) 2022/542 already requires member states to phase out reduced rates on fossil fuels [@VATDirective2022], and a carbon component on domestic heating fuel at a reduced rate would apply only where the forward obligation does not. Whether it reaches zero-rated food is a choice for each member state. Food is 11 percent of household spending, with intensities of 0.42–0.81 kg per euro, so zero-rating it would remove 27 percent of the carbon embodied in the taxable basket.

# Distribution {#sec-distribution}

The swap is mildly regressive within member states and, if the value cut were set EU-wide, would move money from poorer member states to richer ones. Setting the cut nationally avoids the second effect; returning the forward obligation's receipts per household more than offsets the first.

**Prior evidence.** VAT is regressive against income but proportional or progressive against total spending [@Decoster2010]. Household carbon rises with income less than proportionally, with an income elasticity below one [@Sager2019; @LevinsonOBrien2019], so a per-tonne charge takes a larger share of poorer households' spending before revenue is returned. @Feindt2021, who model a comprehensive consumption-based carbon price in 23 EU countries, find it neutral or progressive within most member states but regressive across the EU, because households in eastern member states bear higher average burdens; small transfers between member states would offset that. The claim of v0.1 that the design is "more benign than production-side carbon taxes" does not survive this evidence.

**Method.** I applied the purchasers'-price defaults of @tbl-defaults to Eurostat's household budget survey shares by income quintile for the 22 member states with detailed data [@EurostatHBS], at €200 per tonne and 2022 intensities. The direct emissions reached by the forward obligation are allocated by each quintile's spending on household energy and on fuel for vehicles, using each member state's emissions from heating and transport [@EurostatAEA] and its spending on those items [@EurostatCOICOP]. Each member state cuts its value component to keep the swap neutral. The burden is the full carbon price on every tonne, against no carbon price, so it overstates the change from today by the ETS cost already in prices, and at the central 2037 intensity it would be about half as large. Appendix C lists the simplifications.

| Income quintile | Carbon component (% of spending) | Taxable share of spending (%) | Swap net of national value cut | Obligation (% of spending) | Swap + obligation, returned as VAT cut | Swap + obligation, returned per household |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Poorest fifth | 5.53 | 65.5 | +0.41 | 1.59 | +0.50 | −1.16 |
| Second | 5.47 | 66.9 | +0.24 | 1.65 | +0.36 | −0.31 |
| Third | 5.42 | 68.2 | +0.09 | 1.65 | +0.17 | +0.05 |
| Fourth | 5.38 | 69.3 | −0.04 | 1.60 | −0.03 | +0.23 |
| Richest fifth | 5.25 | 70.3 | −0.24 | 1.48 | −0.38 | +0.29 |

: Net change in taxes by income quintile at €200/tCO₂e and 2022 intensities, percent of household spending; averages of national quintiles in 22 member states, weighted by household spending. Positive values are net losses. Source: author's calculation from @EurostatHBS, @EurostatAEA and @EurostatCOICOP with the defaults of @tbl-defaults; `2.Source/distribution.py`. {#tbl-distribution}

**Results.** The carbon component itself is almost proportional: 5.5 percent of spending for the poorest fifth and 5.3 percent for the richest (@tbl-distribution). The swap is regressive for a different reason. Poorer households spend more of their budget on rent, which is exempt, so they receive less of the value-component cut: the taxable share of spending rises from 65.5 percent in the poorest fifth to 70.3 percent in the richest. Net of the national value cut, the poorest fifth pays 0.41 percent of spending more and the richest 0.24 percent less (@fig-distribution). That spread of 0.65 points is small next to the 5.5 percent of spending that the carbon component reprices. The forward obligation takes about 1.6 percent of spending in every quintile. Returned as a further value cut, it widens the spread slightly; returned as an equal amount per household, it makes the package progressive, with the poorest fifth gaining 1.2 percent of spending and the richest losing 0.3 percent.

![Net change in taxes at €200/tCO₂e and 2022 intensities. A: by income quintile, with the value component cut nationally. B: by member state if the value component were cut by one EU-wide rate. Source: as @tbl-distribution; `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig3-distribution.png){#fig-distribution width=100%}

**Between member states.** Before any revenue is returned, the carbon component takes 7.0 percent of spending in Poland and 6.7 percent in Bulgaria, against 4.5 percent in Luxembourg. If one EU-wide value cut returned the revenue, Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia would lose 0.7–0.8 percent of household spending and Luxembourg and Malta would gain 0.6 percent (@fig-distribution, panel B), the pattern @Feindt2021 find. The neutrality rule avoids this because each member state cuts its own value component by its own receipts. The forward obligation varies more across member states: from 0.7 percent of spending in Finland to 4.0 percent in Croatia and 4.5 percent in Hungary, where household fuel is cheap per tonne of carbon it releases and incomes are lower. The Social Climate Fund, created alongside ETS2 to support vulnerable households [@SCFReg], is the natural channel for part of the obligation's receipts in these member states.

**Targeted rebates.** Three options follow, in order of preference. Return the forward obligation's receipts per household or per person, nationally; @tbl-distribution shows this more than offsets the swap's regressivity. Keep the carbon component on reduced-rate necessities so that the value cut, not an exemption, does the protecting. And present the reform as a cut in VAT on clean goods, because perceived losses drive opposition more than actual ones [@DouenneFabre2022; @Dechezlepretre2025; @Carattini2018].

# The forward obligation on energy suppliers {#sec-obligation}

Fuel burned in homes and vehicles should be priced through a legal obligation on its suppliers, fixed a decade ahead, because those few firms decide the assets that lock in emissions for decades and a tax reset each budget does not move their investment.

**Why VAT cannot reach it.** Households' direct emissions were 706 Mt CO₂e in 2022, 290 Mt from heating and 401 Mt from transport [@EurostatAEA]. That carbon is released when the fuel is burned, after the last sale, so it is not embodied in any good and the carbon component, which prices embodied carbon, misses it. At €200 per tonne it is worth €141 billion a year, 1.7 percent of household spending. Returned equally, that is €316 a year for each of the 446 million EU residents at the start of 2022 [@EurostatPop]. Natural gas emits about 0.20 tCO₂ per MWh [@IPCC2006], so the obligation adds €20 per MWh in 2032 and €40 per MWh in 2037; diesel emits about 2.7 kg per liter, on the IPCC factors and an assumed density of 0.84 kg per liter, so €200 per tonne adds €0.54 per liter. A household that burns 12 MWh of gas a year for heating (stylized) would pay €480 in 2037, more than a person's equal share of the receipts; a household that has switched to a heat pump would pay nothing and receive the share.

**Market structure.** A small number of firms supply these fuels: refiners and fuel importers for road and heating oil, and gas shippers and suppliers for natural gas. They own or contract the refineries, import terminals, pipelines and retail networks, assets that last for decades. Their decisions on refinery conversion, biofuel and hydrogen capacity, and gas network investment fix much of the emissions path to 2050. An obligation that falls on them, not on millions of households, is cheaper to administer and reaches the decision that matters, which is investment.

**Time inconsistency.** A government that announces a rising carbon tax has an incentive to lower it once firms have invested, so firms discount the announcement [@KydlandPrescott1977; @LaffontTirole1996; @HelmHepburnMash2003]. The problem is sharper for an oligopoly: a few large suppliers can lobby to delay a price, and each expects that its own underinvestment raises the political cost of enforcing it. Carbon contracts for difference address the same problem for industrial investment [@ChiappinelliNeuhoff2020]. A forward obligation addresses it for fuel supply. Written into law today, naming the price floor and dates a decade out, it is harder to unwind than a tax rate, because firms will have invested on its terms and repeal would be visible and contested, and it becomes a liability on suppliers' balance sheets now, visible to their auditors and lenders [@Brunner2012; @Nemet2017].

**Design.** Each supplier surrenders one compliance unit for each tonne of CO₂ in the fuel it releases for final use, with a price floor rising €20 a year to €200 per tonne in 2037, in step with the carbon component. An absolute obligation per tonne sold is stronger than an intensity standard, which implicitly subsidizes fuel use [@HollandHughesKnittel2009]. Fuel covered by the obligation is outside the carbon component on the same tonnes; Proposition 3 handles the overlap automatically, because the supplier's invoice carries the price already paid. Electricity suppliers carry no separate obligation: power is a good in the VAT chain, and generators' carbon is priced by the ETS or a power-sector feebate [@CFPB12] and deducted where it is. The final user therefore pays the full consumption price on electricity's carbon through the VAT invoice. In a country without a carbon component in VAT, the same result needs the obligation extended to electricity retailers, net of the generators' price, as paper 1.1 describes [@CFPB11].

**What is new against ETS2 and the Fuel Quality Directive.** The EU already has both precedents. The Fuel Quality Directive obliged fuel suppliers to cut the life-cycle greenhouse gas intensity of their fuel by 6 percent by 2020 [@FQD2009]: an intensity standard, not a price. ETS2 places the compliance obligation on suppliers of fuel for buildings and road transport [@ETS2Dir], the same point of obligation proposed here. Its start has been put back from 2027 to 2028, and it contains a mechanism to release allowances if the price rises above €45 per tonne in 2020 prices [VERIFY: current ETS2 start date and price-containment trigger]. ETS2 therefore gives firms a quantity path and a soft ceiling, but no floor and no price beyond its first years. The forward obligation adds what ETS2 lacks: a published price floor, rising on a fixed path for ten years, written into the Directive. Technically it is ETS2 with an auction reserve price that rises €20 a year; a floor of this kind is the exogenous price element @GoulderSchein2013 favor over a pure cap. Three details complete the design. Allowances that do not sell at the floor are cancelled, so the floor is a price, not a promise to buy. Banking is allowed, so suppliers can hedge the published path. And the law may raise the floor but not lower it before 2037 except by a new act, so the commitment binds in one direction. Coverage follows ETS2: fuel released for consumption in buildings, road transport and small industry, whether refined in the EU or imported, which makes the obligation origin-neutral.

**Interactions.** The obligation's receipts go to member states, as ETS2 auction revenue does, and should be returned per household (@sec-distribution). The obligation does not alter the carbon component on goods. It interacts with the power-sector feebate only through fuel switching: as the gas price rises, heat pumps gain, and electricity demand grows.

# Legal basis {#sec-legal}

The carbon component needs unanimity; the forward obligation does not. This section sets out the settled points, the open ones, and the routes that follow.

**Settled: Article 113 governs a change to VAT.** Article 113 TFEU requires the Council, acting unanimously, to adopt provisions harmonizing "turnover taxes, excise duties and other forms of indirect taxation" [@TFEU]. The VAT Directive defines VAT as "a general tax on consumption exactly proportional to the price of the goods and services" (Article 1(2)) and sets the rate structure in Articles 96–99 [@VATDirective]. A carbon component charged on the VAT invoice and credited in the VAT return changes the base, the rate structure and the deduction rules of that Directive. It is an amendment of harmonized turnover-tax law and needs unanimity.

**Settled: Article 192(2)(a) does not avoid unanimity.** Article 192(1) allows environmental measures by qualified majority, but paragraph 2(a) reserves "provisions primarily of a fiscal nature" to the Council acting unanimously [@TFEU]. v0.1 proposed adopting the carbon component under Article 192 to avoid unanimity. A component of VAT, collected through VAT returns, is hard to describe as anything other than primarily fiscal. The boundary of "primarily fiscal" is contested: @Scuderi2022 argues for reading it so as to admit environmental levies whose main aim is regulatory, but the Court of Justice has not settled the question, and an argument that a VAT component is not primarily fiscal would be a weak foundation for a measure this size.

**The CBAM precedent does not transfer.** CBAM was adopted by qualified majority under Article 192(1) [@CBAMReg] because it is a duty to surrender certificates that mirror the ETS, not a tax. Its price is an allowance price and its collection is outside the tax system. The forward obligation shares that structure; the carbon component does not.

**Open: national routes under Article 401.** Article 401 of the VAT Directive lets a member state maintain or introduce "any taxes, duties or charges which cannot be characterised as turnover taxes", provided they create no border formalities within the EU [@VATDirective]. The Court has read "turnover tax" through the essential characteristics of VAT: general application to transactions in goods and services, proportionality to price, charging at each stage of production and distribution, and deduction of tax paid at earlier stages. A national tax with all four is prohibited; one that lacks one or more may stand [@CJEUBancaPopolare2006; @CJEUDanskDenkavit1992]. A national carbon component designed as in @sec-chain has three of the four, but not, in its verified form, proportionality to price: it is charged per tonne of embodied carbon, like an excise on carbon content. The design choice therefore matters legally. A charge levied per tonne at verified or per-unit default intensity has a defensible claim to fall outside "turnover tax"; one levied as a per-euro rate on the VAT invoice looks like a second VAT and probably does not. This is the open question on which a member state should seek an opinion before legislating.

**Open: the standard-rate floor.** A member state acting alone can lower its standard rate to the 15 percent floor of Article 97 and raise the difference through a carbon charge under Article 401. It cannot go below the floor without a unanimous amendment.

**Routes.** Three follow. *Union route*: the Commission proposes a Directive under Article 113, offering fiscal neutrality and member-state control of the value component to win unanimity; the passerelle in the last subparagraph of Article 192(2), which lets the Council unanimously move a matter to qualified majority, is not a shortcut, because invoking it needs unanimity too. *Coalition route*: willing member states legislate national carbon charges under Article 401, designed per tonne, coordinated on defaults and verification; enhanced cooperation under Article 20 TEU is available but, as the stalled financial transaction tax shows, still needs unanimity among participants and has not delivered a tax [@FTTDecision2013]. *Obligation first*: the forward obligation, a compliance scheme like ETS2 and the Fuel Quality Directive, can be adopted now by qualified majority under Article 192(1) as an amendment to the ETS Directive, which ETS2 already is.

Trade law treats the two parts differently. The forward obligation falls on fuel released for consumption, whether refined in the EU or imported, and prices the carbon in the fuel, a physical property of the product; it raises no like-product question. The carbon component raises the question discussed in @sec-defaults, and a national version raises it in the same form: a member state charging per tonne at defaults the same for every origin treats like products alike, whatever route it takes under EU law.

The materials consumption charge of @Ismer2016 is legally easier than a VAT component: an excise-type liability on a few materials, collected outside VAT, fits the CBAM structure. That is a point against the VAT vehicle for anything to be adopted soon by qualified majority, and in favor of starting with the obligation and a materials charge while the carbon component is negotiated.

# Administration and fraud {#sec-admin}

The carbon component adds a column to the VAT return, not a new tax administration, but it raises the gain from misdeclaring a product's category.

**What changes for firms.** A registered business adds two fields to each invoice, the carbon base and the carbon price already paid, and three to its return: carbon component charged, carbon component credited and net payable. Most firms apply published defaults to their sales by product category, exactly as they apply VAT rates. Importers apply the default at customs clearance, on the customs value, alongside import VAT. Exporters reclaim the component on their inputs. Firms below the VAT registration threshold are outside the system, as for VAT; their purchases carry the carbon component as a cost.

**Where it adds little risk.** The familiar VAT frauds, missing-trader and carousel fraud, exploit the refund of input tax on goods that cross borders [@KeenSmith2006]. The Commission estimates the EU's VAT compliance gap at €128 billion in 2023, 9.5 percent of liability, and the gap from missing-trader intra-community fraud at €12.5–32.8 billion a year between 2010 and 2023 [@VATGap2025]. A carbon column adds proportionately to the stakes in those frauds, by the carbon component's share of the tax, but not a new mechanism. Defaults by customs category are checked against the same codes customs already enforce, and the carbon base on an invoice follows from the category and value already declared.

**Where it adds real risk.** Three points need controls. *Misclassification*: declaring a product in a lower-intensity category, which the carbon component rewards even where VAT rates are the same. At €200 per tonne, moving a good from a category at 0.60 kg per euro to one at 0.30 saves 6 percent of its value. That is less than the gap of ten points or more between standard and reduced VAT rates, over which classification disputes already arise, but it applies across many more product lines. The remedy is the customs classification system and its penalties, plus defaults that do not vary much within a heading. *Rebuttal fraud*: overstated claims of low intensity. Rebuttals should be verified by accredited verifiers under the CBAM rules, audited on a risk basis, and declared at plant or firm level, not per consignment [@Neuhoff2026]. *Refund positions*: where a firm's output base falls below its input base, Proposition 1 implies a refund. Published defaults should be consistent along chains so that this does not arise from the schedule itself, and refund claims should be checked as VAT refund claims are.

**Phasing.** Administration favors a slow start: defaults at the EU average, rebuttal open first to CBAM goods where verification exists, and the carbon price starting at €20 a tonne, at which a misclassification gains little.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

A carbon component credited through the VAT chain charges each firm on the carbon it adds and the consumer on the carbon in the whole supply chain, as VAT does for value. Calibrated on Eurostat's input–output tables, the taxable household basket embodies 0.41 kg CO₂e per euro and imports about twice as much as EU-made goods, so the carbon component reaches the 40 percent of household carbon emitted abroad that the ETS and CBAM do not. A rule that cuts the value component by last year's carbon receipts keeps the swap neutral without a forecast, and setting it nationally avoids transfers between member states. The swap is mildly regressive, and returning the forward obligation's receipts per household more than offsets it. The main limitation is legal: the carbon component needs unanimity, or a national design per tonne that the Court has not tested. The next steps are a legal opinion on that design, a default schedule at Combined Nomenclature level, and the forward obligation as an amendment to ETS2 with a price floor to 2037.

# Appendix A: Literature review {.unnumbered}

This appendix reviews the literature by theme. It draws on a separate review of 55 works; where only an abstract or the bibliographic record could be checked, the text says what the work addresses rather than what it finds.

**A.1 Destination and origin bases, and VAT.** The equivalence of origin- and destination-based commodity taxes is old: for a uniform, broad-based tax with balanced trade, switching the basis changes price levels and exchange rates but not trade, production or consumption [@LockwoodDeMezaMyles1994]. @LockwoodWhalley2010 apply the result to carbon border adjustments and argue that the policy debate confuses price-level effects with relative-price effects. The result cuts both ways for this paper. It explains why the VAT machinery adjusts for borders without extra apparatus, which is the practical case for using it. It also shows that VAT's value component, being uniform, carries no carbon incentive and no trade advantage: everything that matters for carbon and for trade sits in the carbon component. The World Bank's total carbon price takes the same view. @Agnolucci2023 compute direct and indirect carbon prices for 142 countries over 1991–2021 and exclude general VAT because, as across-the-board consumption taxes, VATs "do not affect relative prices"; only VAT preferences on fuels enter, as subsidies. The arithmetic that a 15 percent VAT on a good embodying 0.30 kg per euro is "worth" €500 per tonne is correct, but it is not a carbon price in any useful sense, and version 0.1's claim that the World Bank counts VAT as one was wrong.

VAT's spread and administrative maturity are documented by @KeenLockwood2010 and @KeenLockwood2006, the second on whether VAT raised total revenue. Destination-based business taxation rests on the same logic as VAT: a tax levied where the immobile consumer is removes the incentive to shift profits or production [@Devereux2021; @Auerbach2017]. @Shapiro2021 adds an observation that sharpens the case for a destination charge on carbon: tariffs and non-tariff barriers are lower on dirty industries than on clean ones, which amounts to an implicit global subsidy to CO₂ in traded goods of \$550–800 billion a year. The existing destination-side tax on trade already prices embodied carbon negatively.

**A.2 Consumption-based accounting.** Production-based inventories, which national targets use, attribute emissions to the country where they occur; consumption-based accounts attribute them to the country of final demand [@PetersHertwich2008]. Emissions from producing traded goods grew from 4.3 GtCO₂ (20 percent of the global total) in 1990 to 7.8 GtCO₂ (26 percent) in 2008, and net transfers from developing to developed countries grew from 0.4 to 1.6 GtCO₂, more than the Kyoto Protocol's reductions [@Peters2011]. In 2004, 23 percent of global CO₂ was embodied in trade, and more than 30 percent of consumption-based emissions were imported in Switzerland, Sweden, Austria, the United Kingdom and France [@DavisCaldeira2010]. @Grubb2022 find that net transfers peaked around 2006 and have declined since.

Two qualifications matter. @JakobSteckelEdenhofer2014 argue that a tonne of imported embodied emissions is not a tonne added to global emissions, so pricing all embodied carbon at the full social cost is not first-best; trade measures should concentrate on a few emissions-intensive, highly traded industries. And @Steininger2014 compare the justice and cost-effectiveness of consumption- and production-based approaches for a region acting alone. This paper therefore rests the case for a consumption charge on leakage, administration and acceptability, not on first-best optimality.

**A.3 Consumption charges: the closest prior work.** A European proposal for a consumption charge on carbon-intensive materials, sometimes called a climate contribution, is the nearest relative of the carbon component. @Ismer2016 set out its legal design as an excise-type liability on materials such as steel and cement, at benchmark intensity, applying equally to domestic and imported products. @PollittNeuhoffLin2020 simulate it with the E3ME model: levied at the level of the free allocation that heavy industry receives, at about €80/tCO₂ it cuts energy-related CO₂ by about 6 percent and process emissions by up to 40 percent by 2050, roughly 10 percent of total EU CO₂, with a small rise in GDP, a small fall in employment and no leakage. @Grubb2022 place the charge among three trade-compatible price options (border adjustments, a carbon-footprint consumption charge, and an excise contribution combined with free allocation). They note that a charge on actual footprints would reward exporters who decarbonize, but that tracing embodied carbon through global value chains is administratively demanding and open to fraud; defaults by product category are a feasible shortcut if they apply to imports and domestic goods alike. @Neuhoff2026 restate the idea for the CBAM era: CBAM's production-specific intensities invite resource shuffling, as foreign producers send their cleanest output to the EU, and leave value-chain and export leakage unaddressed; they propose a standardized liability per tonne of material, independent of process and origin, applied along the value chain with export relief.

Formal analysis of footprint taxes predates these proposals. @McAuslandNajjar2015 analyze a retail tax on carbon footprints falling on domestic and imported goods alike, and @McAusland2021 returns to footprint leakage under carbon taxes. @EichnerPethig2015 and @EichnerPethig2015b compare unilateral production- and consumption-based carbon taxes and show that a consumption-based tax can produce negative leakage in general equilibrium. @Holland2012 shows that, when regulation is incomplete and leakage is possible, an intensity standard combined with a consumption tax can reach the first best, and notes that a consumption tax does not violate trade law: the formal case for pairing the consumption track with an intensity-based production track.

What this paper adds to this line is the vehicle and the scope: the VAT invoice chain with credit for input carbon, which makes each firm pay on the carbon it adds, extends the charge from a handful of materials to every taxable good and service, and gives the destination basis and export relief that the materials charge must build separately.

**A.4 Border adjustment, trade law and trading partners.** The design literature establishes the main choices for border carbon adjustment: sectoral coverage, the measure of embodied carbon (domestic benchmark, country default or firm data), treatment of exports, and recognition of foreign policy [@IsmerNeuhoff2007; @Mehling2019; @KeenParryRoaf2022]. @Mehling2019 give the fullest legal analysis, under GATT Articles I, II:2(a), III and XX and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, and recommend narrow coverage, default values with a right of rebuttal and crediting of foreign policies; they leave open whether carbon intensity can differentiate like products under Article III:2. @IsmerNeuhoff2007 argue that border adjustment at the intensity of the best available technology is defensible. @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend benchmarking first on domestic intensities and moving to country-specific values later, with rebuttal, and note the tension between destination-basis border adjustment and the origin-basis accounting of the Paris Agreement.

The evidence on trading partners favors one default for every origin. @Mattoo2009 find that a border tax on the carbon content of imports, measured at the exporter's own intensity across all merchandise, would cut China's manufacturing exports by about a fifth and low- and middle-income countries' exports by 8 percent, with real income losses of 3.7 and 2.4 percent, while a tax based on the carbon content of domestic production would do far less damage. @CBAMExposure2025 find macroeconomic exposure to CBAM small for most countries and high for a few, such as Mozambique through aluminum; their method could size partners' exposure to an economy-wide carbon component. @Evans2021 show that a border adjustment on imports alone leaves exporters exposed and that export relief raises legal risk, which careful design can reduce; a VAT-based charge zero-rates exports by construction.

**A.5 Leakage.** Model-based studies find leakage of 5–25 percent without border adjustment and −5 to 15 percent with it; some leakage survives border adjustment through the fossil-fuel price channel [@BrangerQuirion2014]. Ex-post studies find no detectable leakage from the EU ETS up to about 2014 [@NaegeleZaklan2019; @Dechezlepretre2022], partly because industry was shielded by free allocation [@Grubb2022]. Two consequences follow for this paper. The claim that a destination charge is leakage-proof holds for the goods channel only: a charge that lowers EU fossil demand still lowers world fuel prices and raises fuel use elsewhere. And the case for a consumption charge concerns the carbon prices of €100–200 per tonne in prospect, not the leakage observed at the prices of the past.

**A.6 Distribution and acceptability.** Household carbon is a necessity. Environmental Engel curves for the United States show household CO₂ rising with income but less than proportionally [@Sager2019], and the same holds for local air pollutants, with curves shifting down over time [@LevinsonOBrien2019]. A uniform per-tonne charge on consumption therefore takes a larger share of poorer households' spending before revenue is returned. VAT itself is regressive against income but proportional or progressive against total spending [@Decoster2010]. The most directly relevant study is @Feindt2021, who model a comprehensive carbon price on all goods, including imported ones, in 23 EU countries: incidence before recycling is mostly neutral, sometimes progressive, within countries, but regressive across the EU, because households in lower-income, mainly eastern, member states bear higher average burdens; relatively small transfers between member states would offset this. @sec-distribution reproduces both patterns with independent data.

Acceptability depends on perceptions as much as on incidence. After the Yellow Vests protests, most French respondents rejected a tax-and-dividend scheme, overestimated their own losses and wrongly believed it regressive, and information moved beliefs only slightly [@DouenneFabre2022]. Across 20 countries, support for climate policies depends on perceived effectiveness, perceived personal losses and concern for poorer households [@Dechezlepretre2025]. @Carattini2018 identify five sources of resistance to carbon taxes (personal cost, regressivity, economic damage, doubts about effectiveness and suspicion of a revenue grab) and remedies including phasing, earmarking, lump-sum rebates and communication. @Klenert2018 address the design of revenue use for public support. A revenue-neutral swap phased over ten years answers the revenue-grab and personal-cost concerns; presenting it as a cut in VAT on clean goods answers the effectiveness concern.

**A.7 Credibility and forward commitment.** Optimal plans are time-inconsistent when agents' expectations depend on future policy [@KydlandPrescott1977]. In environmental policy, a regulator that cannot commit to future permit supply weakens the incentive to innovate [@LaffontTirole1996]. @HelmHepburnMash2003 apply the problem to carbon and propose delegating carbon policy to an independent agency; @Brunner2012 compare commitment devices, including legislation, delegation, contracts and reputation; @Nemet2017 address credibility problems for low-carbon investment. @ChiappinelliNeuhoff2020 show that carbon contracts for difference, in which the government pays investors a fixed carbon price, improve decarbonization incentives and derive conditions under which the government is willing to tie its hands. On instrument choice, exogenous pricing through a tax or a cap with a price floor or ceiling avoids price volatility and harmful interactions with other policies [@GoulderSchein2013], building on the prices-versus-quantities comparison of @Weitzman1974 and @Pizer2002. The forward obligation of @sec-obligation applies these ideas to ETS2: it is an application, not a new mechanism, and its novelty is the published floor fixed a decade ahead.

**A.8 Feebates and the production track.** Feebates price intensity without raising average costs. @Johnson2006 sets out the instrument, @SternerIsaksson2006 analyze Sweden's refunded NOₓ charge, a working revenue-neutral feebate, and @DHaultfoeuille2014 study France's car bonus-malus, which shifted purchases toward low-CO₂ cars. @GoulderParry2008 compare environmental instruments against cost-effectiveness, equity, uncertainty and political feasibility and conclude that no instrument dominates; they do not discuss feebates, contrary to version 0.1. Whether @FischerNewell2008 support version 0.1's claim about feebates could not be checked; the claim is dropped. Intensity standards, the regulatory cousin of feebates, implicitly subsidize output and can even raise emissions [@HollandHughesKnittel2009]; the consumption track exists to supply the output margin they miss [@CFPB11; @CFPB12].

**A.9 Where the paper sits.** Three literatures meet in the carbon consumption tax. From destination-based taxation it takes the VAT machinery and the insight that only the carbon component changes relative prices. From the consumption-charge literature it takes the default-intensity approach and the case for applying it equally to every origin, and adds the VAT invoice chain with credit for input carbon. From the credibility literature it takes the case for a forward-dated obligation on fuel suppliers. The distributional evidence qualifies version 0.1: a consumption charge is mildly regressive before recycling and, with EU-wide recycling, regressive across member states. The new elements are the VAT-chain implementation and its three propositions, the neutrality rule, product-category defaults calibrated from input–output data, and the pairing with a forward obligation on fuels that never enter a goods chain. Appendix D records the corrections to version 0.1.

# Appendix B: Proofs {.unnumbered}

*Setup.* Stages $k = 1, \dots, n$; $p_k = p_{k-1} + w_k$ with $p_0 = 0$; $E_k = \sum_{j \le k} a_j$ with $E_0 = 0$; carbon base $C_k$ with $C_0 = 0$; remittance $T_k$ as in @eq-remit. Prices are cost plus value added; taxes are passed to the next stage, except that an exempt firm's irrecoverable input taxes become part of its price.

*Proposition 1.* (i) $\sum_{k=1}^n T_k = v \sum_k (p_k - p_{k-1}) + P \sum_k (C_k - C_{k-1}) = v\,p_n + P\,C_n$, because both sums telescope; nothing depends on $C_1, \dots, C_{n-1}$. (ii) With $C_k = E_k$, the carbon part of $T_k$ is $P(E_k - E_{k-1}) = P\,a_k$. (iii) The consumer pays $p_n + v\,p_n + P\,C_n$; with $C_n = E_n$ the carbon part is $P\,E_n$.

*Proposition 2.* Let stage $j$ be exempt. It remits nothing and pays $v\,p_{j-1} + P\,C_{j-1}$ to its supplier without credit, so its price is $p^x_j = p_{j-1} + w_j + v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}$ when $C_{j-1} = E_{j-1}$. (i) If $j = n$, the consumer pays $p^x_n = p_n + v\,p_{n-1} + P\,E_{n-1}$ and no further tax. Against full crediting, $(1+v)\,p_n + P\,E_n$, the difference is $-v\,w_n - P\,a_n$: value added and carbon added at the exempt stage go untaxed, and upstream carbon is charged once. (ii) If $j < n$, every later price is higher by $\Delta = v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}$, and stage $j+1$ has no creditable input tax, so the taxes on later invoices are $v$ and $P\,C_k$ on the full values and bases. The consumer pays $(1+v)(p_n + \Delta) + P\,E_n$, which exceeds the full-crediting outlay by $(1+v)\,\Delta = (1+v)(v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1})$. The upstream carbon $E_{j-1}$ is charged once inside $\Delta$ and again inside $E_n$.

*Proposition 3.* With $Q_k = \sum_{j \le k} \min(q_j, P)\, a_j$ and carbon component $P\,E_k - Q_k$ on each sale, firm $k$ remits $(P\,E_k - Q_k) - (P\,E_{k-1} - Q_{k-1}) = (P - \min(q_k, P))\,a_k \ge 0$. Each tonne emitted at stage $k$ bears $q_k$ directly and $P - \min(q_k, P)$ through the carbon component, a total of $\max(P, q_k)$. Summed over the chain, the carbon component raises $P\,E_n - Q_n$ and explicit prices raise $\sum_k q_k a_k$, which equals $P\,E_n$ when every $q_k \le P$. For a revenue-neutral feebate the sector-average net price is zero, so it contributes nothing to $Q$ and the consumer bears $P\,E_n$ through the carbon component.

All three results were checked symbolically for $n = 4$ with sympy, and the worked example of @sec-chain numerically, in `2.Source/check_propositions.py`.

![Value component, ETS price and carbon component remitted at each stage of the worked example in @sec-chain. Source: `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig4-vat-chain.png){#fig-chain width=90%}

# Appendix C: Calibration of defaults and distribution {.unnumbered}

*Data.* (1) FIGARO inter-country input–output table at basic prices, product by product, 2022, million euro [@EurostatFIGARO]: 50 economies (45 named countries plus the rest of the world and four Western Balkan economies) by 64 CPA products, with five categories of final demand. (2) Greenhouse gas emissions by emitting country and NACE A*64 industry, thousand tonnes CO₂e, from the footprint dataset with destination "world" and all final demand [@EurostatGHGFP]; the CO₂-only dataset gives the last column of @tbl-defaults. (3) Household direct emissions from heating and transport [@EurostatAEA]. (4) Household budget shares by income quintile, 2020 wave, and mean expenditure by quintile [@EurostatHBS]. (5) Household final consumption by COICOP purpose, 2022 [@EurostatCOICOP]. All were downloaded from the Eurostat API on 29 October 2026.

*Model.* With intermediate flows $Z$, output $x$ and technical coefficients $A = Z \hat{x}^{-1}$, emission intensities per euro of output $s = f \hat{x}^{-1}$, where industry emissions $f$ are assigned to the matching CPA product, the multipliers are $m = s\,(I - A)^{-1}$, in kg CO₂e per euro of final demand. The four Western Balkan economies, present in FIGARO but not in the emissions data, take the rest-of-world intensity for each product; they are a negligible share of EU purchases. Category intensities weight $m$ by EU-27 household final consumption by origin and product. The model gives an EU-27 footprint of 3,749 Mt CO₂e for all final demand excluding households' direct emissions, against Eurostat's 3,743 Mt; for households alone, 2,282 Mt against 2,255 Mt; for CO₂ alone, 2,760 Mt against 2,797 Mt.

*Purchasers' prices.* Household purchases of trade services (CPA G45–G47), €1.19 trillion, are 64.5 percent of household purchases of goods (CPA A–C) at basic prices, €1.85 trillion. Spreading them evenly gives a goods intensity at purchasers' prices of $(e_g + 0.645\, e_{\text{trade}})/1.645$. Taxes on products are excluded throughout.

*Sources of the footprint.* Of the 2,116 Mt CO₂e embodied in taxable household purchases, 28 percent was emitted by EU power and energy-intensive industry (CPA D35, C17, C19, C20, C23, C24, a proxy for ETS coverage), 14 percent by EU agriculture, 17 percent by other EU industries and services, and 40 percent outside the EU (`2.Source/footprint_sources.csv`).

*Distribution.* COICOP 3-digit purposes are mapped to the categories of @tbl-defaults (`2.Source/distribution.py`); rents, health and education services, social protection, insurance and finance are exempt. Household energy (COICOP 04.5) carries the embodied intensity of electricity and gas supply per euro of EU spending on it, 0.83 kg CO₂e per euro; fuel for vehicles (07.2) carries the supply-chain intensity of refined petroleum products per euro of spending on it, 0.25 kg per euro. Direct emissions per euro of 04.5 and 07.2 spending are computed for each member state. Simplifications: budget shares are applied to spending including taxes; every member state uses EU-wide defaults; national quintiles are averaged with household-spending weights rather than ranked EU-wide; the 2020 survey wave is combined with 2022 intensities.

*Code.* `2.Source/calibrate_defaults.py` builds the model and writes `defaults_by_category.csv`, `defaults_by_product.csv`, `basket_summary.csv` and `footprint_sources.csv`; `2.Source/distribution.py` writes the distribution files; `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py` prints the fiscal numbers and draws @fig-defaults, @fig-rule, @fig-distribution and @fig-chain. The input–output download is about 72 MB and is cached outside the repository. Setting the environment variable `CCT_YEAR=2023` reruns the calibration for 2023, which gives a taxable basket intensity of 0.36 kg CO₂e per euro.

# Appendix D: What held from version 0.1 {.unnumbered}

Version 0.1's arithmetic held; most of its data and two of its design choices did not. The recomputation is in `1.Presentation/figures/make_figures.py` and, for the data, in this paper's calibration.

*What held.* The break-even intensity of the illustrative path is 0.25 kg per euro. On v0.1's assumed intensities, EU producers at 0.20 falling to 0.15 kg per euro end at 13.0 percent in 2037, and Chinese exporters at 0.40 falling to 0.25 peak at 15.75 percent in 2032 (v0.1: 15.8) and return to 15.0 percent. The share of consumption outside VAT, which v0.1 put at 35–40 percent, is 31 percent of household spending at basic prices (@tbl-defaults).

*What did not hold.* (1) Intensities: v0.1 assumed 0.15–0.25 kg CO₂ per euro for EU manufactured goods and 0.35–0.45 for Chinese ones, without a source. The calibration gives 0.26–0.73 kg CO₂e per euro for EU-made manufactures and 0.68–1.94 for Chinese-made ones at basic prices (`2.Source/defaults_by_category.csv`), with ratios mostly between 2 and 4, not 1.5 to 2 (on a CO₂-only basis all figures are lower, as @tbl-defaults shows). (2) The fiscal base: v0.1 used a €9 trillion base at 0.30 kg per euro. Taxable household spending was €5.1 trillion at basic prices in 2022, so half a point of VAT is worth €26 billion, not €45 billion, and €20 per tonne raises €42 billion gross, not €55–65 billion. (3) Neutrality: v0.1 called the fixed path approximately neutral; @tbl-fiscal shows it can lose or gain over €100 billion a year by 2037. (4) Country scores: v0.1's one score per exporting country gave no signal between products and set different rates on like products by origin; this paper replaces it with product-category defaults the same for every origin. (5) Legal basis: v0.1's adoption under Article 192 by qualified majority is replaced by the analysis of @sec-legal. (6) Citations: the World Bank's total carbon price excludes general VAT [@Agnolucci2023]; the 2025 global average carbon price is about \$5, not €3 [@WorldBank2025]; the social cost of carbon of @Rennert2022 is \$185 per tonne, not \$170; Goulder and Parry (2008) do not discuss feebates [@GoulderParry2008]; Weitzman's uniform-price paper is 2014 [@Weitzman2014]; the 2021 destination-based cash-flow tax chapter is by @Devereux2021; and the "carbon-added tax" of Courchene and Allan (2009) could not be found. Version 0.1's Phase Two (an upstream carbon tax and a Carbon Central Bank from 2037) is outside the scope of this paper.
